title: The Reemergence of the Big Four in Law
pub: The Practice — Reemergence of the Big Four in Law
author: David B. Wilkins · María J. Esteban Ferrer

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk
st.an: The source addresses how the Big Four may reshape corporate legal services and calls for scrutiny of stakeholder responses. It does not assess AI-driven workforce restructuring, junior-pipeline risks, productivity, displacement, or training, so its position on the cluster’s proposition cannot be determined.
qs: For now, we simply conclude by urging both practitioners and commentators to pay greater attention to what these important players are doing—and, equally as important, to what law firms, clients, and regulators are, or should be, doing in response.

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s business-model framing and materially extends it through the Big Four example: integrated multidisciplinary delivery, process management, IT, global client relationships and business expertise can create competitive advantage beyond adopting technology alone. It also reinforces provider convergence and client demand for value, while appropriately qualifying whether the Big Four can execute this model and how technology will affect their legal businesses.
qs: This new approach, in turn, dovetailed with the Big Four’s own organizational transformation from multidisciplinary firms, offering a variety of separate service lines, to integrated problem-solving networks with deep industry expertise.

To the extent that the world of law is increasingly turning to traditional business methods such as unbundling, outsourcing, process management, and partnering to reduce costs and increase effectiveness, the legal networks of the global accounting firms have a distinct advantage.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source extends the cluster’s operating-model and provider-boundary claims by documenting a pre-generative-AI shift toward multidisciplinary, process- and technology-enabled legal delivery by the Big Four. It shows that redesign, integration and business methods can alter legal competition independently of any claim of general technological competence, while cautioning that advertised capabilities do not verify delivery or quality.
qs: The overall result is a clear effort to move away from the old strategy of law as a separate and largely independent service line and to embrace the vision of legal services as part of a globally integrated business solution for global clients.

To the extent that the world of law is increasingly turning to traditional business methods such as unbundling, outsourcing, process management, and partnering to reduce costs and increase effectiveness, the legal networks of the global accounting firms have a distinct advantage.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s workflow-unbundling proposition and materially extends it through a pre-AI account of the Big Four as integrated, multidisciplinary competitors. It argues that process management, IT capability, global reach and industry-focused organization position these providers to capture recurring legal work that law firms deprioritize, while acknowledging that promoted capabilities and future market reshaping were not fully verified.
qs: To the extent that the world of law is increasingly turning to traditional business methods such as unbundling, outsourcing, process management, and partnering to reduce costs and increase effectiveness, the legal networks of the global accounting firms have a distinct advantage.

This new approach, in turn, dovetailed with the Big Four’s own organizational transformation from multidisciplinary firms, offering a variety of separate service lines, to integrated problem-solving networks with deep industry expertise.

st.t: Big Four: Integration matters more than replacement
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central framing: the Big Four’s legal resurgence is based on integrating law into broader global business solutions, enabled by organizational capabilities and selective regulatory openings. It predicts growth but expressly leaves seamless delivery and eventual dominance uncertain, so it does not claim inevitable law-firm replacement.
qs: However, over the last decade the Big Four accounting firms have quietly rebuilt their legal networks, integrating these services into a new model of “globally integrated business solutions,” and aggressively promoting this model in important emerging economies in Asia-Pacific, Latin America, Africa, and the Middle East.

It is still unclear whether any of the Big Four will be able to fulfill their ambitions of building, as Alexandru Reff, partner-in-charge of Deloitte’s Romanian tax and legal practice, confidently declared in 2013: “the largest legal network in the world.” It is, after all, far easier to promise seamless global multidisciplinary services than it is to deliver them.

kp.k: Big Four legal networks survived and expanded after SOX
kp.d: This January/February 2016 article provides historical legal-market evidence rather than findings about AI. The authors argue that, contrary to widespread expectations following accounting scandals and regulatory reforms, Deloitte, PwC, KPMG and EY rebuilt legal networks with broader geographic reach and practices extending beyond tax into compliance, finance, M&A and employment law.
qs: Far from dying, in recent years the legal service lines linked to the international accountancy networks have grown significantly in size, scope, and importance.

Although tax-related advisory services remain an important cornerstone, the Big Four legal networks are now important players in a broad range of legal fields, including premium and fast-growing practices such as compliance, finance, M&A, and employment law.

kp.k: Website research measures presentation, not verified service delivery
kp.d: The study examined corporate and affiliated-law-firm websites from July 2011 to March 2012, including 491 location sites: 151 PwC, 123 Deloitte, 102 KPMG and 115 EY. It supplemented these with Google searches and legal, accountancy and economic press, then repeated the search in November 2015. The authors explicitly distinguish documented promotional claims and ambitions from evidence that services were actually delivered or were high quality.
qs: Thus, in addition to examining each of the Big Four’s main websites, we also investigated a total of 491 location sites (151 PwC, 123 Deloitte, 102 KPMG, and 115 EY).
In November 2015 we repeated the entire search process to determine what, if anything, had changed since 2012.

We therefore make no representation, for example, about whether the legal services that the Big Four claim to offer in any particular legal market are, in fact, being delivered, or whether their legal work is high quality.

kp.k: Promoted legal services reached extensive international markets
kp.d: In spring 2012, PwC promoted legal services in 124 countries, Deloitte in 97, KPMG in 73 and EY in 29. The authors distinguish 'legal territories' (LTs), advertising a broad range of legal services, from jurisdictions with only 'some reference' to law (SRs), often primarily tax-related. They report expansion beyond Europe into Asia-Pacific, Latin America and Africa; these figures describe advertised presence, not independently confirmed operations.
qs: In the spring of 2012, PwC was promoting legal services in 124 countries worldwide, Deloitte in 97 countries, KPMG in 73 countries, and EY in 29 countries.
Moreover, in the majority (and in the case of EY, the overwhelming majority) of these jurisdictions, the Big Four claimed to be offering a wide range of legal services

kp.k: Integration replaced imitation of freestanding law firms
kp.d: The authors contrast the 1990s strategy of presenting accounting-linked legal networks as traditional law firms with a later strategy of integrating law into multidisciplinary business solutions. In March 2012, websites in 56 percent of PwC LTs, 65 percent of Deloitte LTs and 59 percent of KPMG LTs identified no freestanding legal provider. Even separately presented law firms commonly advertised alliances with the wider network.
qs: The strategy was simple: look as much like a traditional law firm as possible.

as of March 2012, in the majority of PwC LTs (56 percent), Deloitte LTs (65 percent), and KPMG LTs (59 percent), legal practices appeared on the web with no mention of any particular freestanding law firm or legal services firm as providing these services.

The overall result is a clear effort to move away from the old strategy of law as a separate and largely independent service line and to embrace the vision of legal services as part of a globally integrated business solution for global clients.

kp.d: The authors report initially limited visibility: 54 percent of LTs were accessible only through a tax or tax-and-legal service line, and global annual reports in 2011 and 2012 did not reference legal services. PwC adopted more explicit global legal branding first; by June 2015 the others followed. By November 2015, EY's number of broad-service legal territories had increased by 200 percent since March 2012, with 20 percent in Africa and the Middle East and 14 percent in Asia-Pacific.
qs: Finally, in 2011 and 2012, there was no reference concerning the provision of legal services in any of the Big Four’s global annual reports.
By June 2015, Deloitte, EY, and KPMG had all joined PwC in giving global visibility to their extensive legal expertise in all areas of business-related law.

Most notably, since March 2012, EY has increased by 200 percent the number of countries where its member firms offer a wide range of LTs, thus shifting from the almost exclusive location of LTs in Europe (figure 2) to having 20 percent of LTs in Africa and the Middle East, and 14 percent in Asia-Pacific.

kp.k: Lateral recruitment supported expansion alongside internal leadership
kp.d: The article documents recruitment of senior lawyers from traditional firms, including EY's hiring of Freshfields' Richard Norbruis, PwC's hiring of Nikolaus Schrader and Tony O’Malley, and KPMG's hiring of DLA Piper's David Morris. The authors contrast these external hires with internally developed global network leaders, interpreting the latter as a commitment to multidisciplinary integration. They also describe rebranding and integration of affiliated law firms into Big Four networks.
qs: To support this expansion, the Big Four have returned to the kind of lateral recruiting of star lawyers not seen since the 1990s.

the fact that each of the global leaders of the Big Four’s legal networks have all grown up inside these organizations underscores their strong commitment to integrating these practices into the broader culture and practices of their global multidisciplinary network.

kp.k: Auditor restrictions left substantial opportunities for legal expansion
kp.d: The authors argue that SOX section 201 did not impose an audit-only model: it prohibited specified nonaudit services for U.S.-listed audit clients while permitting preapproved tax and other allowable services. Ambiguous boundaries between audit, consulting and law preserved advisory opportunities. Crucially, restrictions on services to audit clients did not prevent targeting companies a network did not audit; the authors identify those clients as the engine of legal-practice growth. They also attribute expansion elsewhere to uneven or ambiguous national restrictions.
qs: Contrary to popular perception, section 201 of SOX did not establish an audit-only rule for the accounting firms.
More importantly, even those nonaudit services that are acknowledged to fall under SOX are prohibited only for a Big Four firm’s own audit clients.
These nonaudit clients have become the engine of growth for the Big Four’s legal practices.

kp.k: Ownership reforms and regulatory ambiguities enabled alternative providers
kp.d: The article describes the Legal Services Act of 2007 reforms in England and Wales as authorizing alternative business structures and multidisciplinary practices, with independent oversight of legal regulators. It reports that PwC, KPMG and EY applied for ABS status in 2013–2014, and that EY and KPMG had received multidisciplinary licenses. Separately, the authors identify regulatory ambiguity in emerging markets, citing Deloitte's promotion of legal services through China's Qin Li Law Firm despite restrictions on foreign law-firm investment and control.
qs: These reforms expressly authorized ABSs and MDPs and removed self-regulation in the legal profession by creating an independent body to oversee legal regulators in England and Wales.

Significantly, two of the three—EY and KPMG—have now been granted an ABS license to become a multidisciplinary professional service firm, under which they are now entitled to provide a mix of legal and nonlegal services to clients.
there are no regulations expressly restricting the form or nature of cooperation between a Chinese law firm and an international accounting firm.

kp.k: Law firms' deregulation advocacy may strengthen Big Four competitors
kp.d: The authors argue that accounting networks' advocacy for removing international barriers to professional services was increasingly echoed by large law firms. They describe U.K. firms lobbying for changes involving conflicts, nonlawyer hiring and compensation, Swiss vereins and outside capital, with U.S. firms beginning to follow. Their interpretation is that these developments make law firms resemble the Big Four while lacking equally developed organizational forms.
qs: the large accountancy networks have played a key role in framing this debate by actively pushing to eliminate global barriers to trade and investment in professional services.
All these changes have made large law firms look more and more like the Big Four—only with an organizational form that is not nearly as well developed.

kp.k: Premium-only strategies ceded recurring work and industry expertise
kp.d: The authors contend that large law firms' focus on high-margin, company-critical deals and litigation left recurring and commodity work available to the Big Four. They attribute the latter's advantage to treating legal matters as elements of broader business strategy, supported by industry expertise, process management, IT capabilities and global delivery. This is the authors' explanation of competitive positioning, not a measured causal estimate.
qs: The mantra for international law firms has been “premium work for premium clients,” thereby leading many firms to exit the commodity businesses in order to concentrate on high-margin assignments.
By targeting only “bet the company” deals and litigation, however, top law firms unwittingly ceded the battle for industry expertise to the Big Four
Leveraging their skill in process management and IT expertise across their increasingly large global footprint, the Big Four easily moved into spaces that the law firms were abandoning.

kp.k: Multidisciplinary organization changes lawyers' roles and client proposition
kp.d: The article describes lawyers simultaneously belonging to legal service lines, industry groups, geographic units and client teams, interacting with tax, consulting, accounting and finance professionals. The authors argue that sophisticated client management and cross-network risk management support integrated solutions. They associate the post-2008 environment with corporate demand for advisers who understand business and offer value for money, and argue that the Big Four recognized this demand faster than law firms.
qs: lawyers working in the Big Four legal practices worldwide play multiple roles simultaneously—as part of the legal service line, an industry group, a particular geographic location, and a number of client teams
clients increasingly cherished this partnering approach, requesting legal advisors that understand the company’s business and provide “value for money.”
The Big Four understood this demand far more quickly than law firms.

kp.k: Talent development forms part of the competitive model
kp.d: The authors argue that the Big Four recognized the need for robust systems to attract, retain and develop professionals more quickly than law firms. They present global teaming and workplace culture as recruitment advantages in the legal market, but provide no comparative retention rates or training-outcome measures in this article.
qs: the Big Four have been far quicker to realize that to remain globally competitive, they needed to develop a model for attracting, retaining, and developing human capital that is as well thought out and robust as their model for delivering high-quality services to clients.

kp.k: Market scale and fragmentation incentivized legal-services investment
kp.d: Citing published estimates, the authors report 72 percent global legal-market growth between 2005 and 2014 to US$616.4 billion, three times the audit market's value. They contrast the Big Four's 23 percent share of global audit turnover in 2014 with the Am Law 100's combined 13 percent share of the global legal market. Their illustration that a 1 percent share of the forecast $726.2 billion legal market in 2019 would make one network the largest legal-services organization is conditional, not a prediction that this share would be attained.
qs: According to published estimates, the global legal services market grew 72 percent between 2005 and 2014, reaching a total value of US$616.4 billion.

While the Big Four’s joint turnover for audits in 2014 represents 23 percent of the value of global audits, the turnover jointly generated by all of the top law firms ranked in the Am Law 100 for the same year accounted for a scant 13 percent of the global legal market.

if any of the Big Four were to capture even a 1 percent share of the global legal market’s forecasted value of $726.2 billion for 2019, that one network would become the largest legal services organization worldwide by far.

kp.k: Technology alliances offered prospective advantages, not demonstrated legal outcomes
kp.d: The authors describe PwC's 2014 Google for Work relationship and EY's LinkedIn alliance involving social and data analytics. They anticipate preparation for technological disruption but explicitly state that consequences for legal businesses remain unknown. These are technology-strategy examples, not evidence of AI deployment or its effects on lawyers.
qs: In 2014, PwC announced its joint business relationship with Google for Work to cocreate solutions for clients.
More recently, EY has established an alliance with LinkedIn designed to “help companies develop deeper and more trusted customer relationships through the use of social and data analytics.”
How these moves are going to impact their global legal businesses is yet to be seen.

kp.k: Consultant-style legal work may favor integrated professional-service networks
kp.d: The article reports Robert Eli Rosen's 2002 hypothesis that in-house counsel and outside firms were becoming consultants integrating legal knowledge into cross-functional business teams. The authors argue that subsequent economic and regulatory changes strengthened this trend, and that unbundling, outsourcing, process management and partnering favor the Big Four's established capabilities. They do not resolve Rosen's concern about the implications for lawyer professionalism.
qs: Robert Eli Rosen hypothesized that changes in the corporate market for legal services were turning both in-house counsel and outside firms into just another “consultant” whose primary task is to integrate legal knowledge into cross-functional teams to better achieve business objectives.

To the extent that the world of law is increasingly turning to traditional business methods such as unbundling, outsourcing, process management, and partnering to reduce costs and increase effectiveness, the legal networks of the global accounting firms have a distinct advantage.

kp.k: Future dominance remains conditional and professional consequences unresolved
kp.d: The authors expect regulatory liberalization, globalization and demand for integrated solutions to support further growth, but caution that promising seamless multidisciplinary services is easier than delivering them and that legal practice and regulation remain substantially local and lawyer-controlled. They leave effects on professionalism, client service and public policy unresolved and recommend closer attention from practitioners and commentators to Big Four activity and responses by firms, clients and regulators.
qs: It is, after all, far easier to promise seamless global multidisciplinary services than it is to deliver them.
And it remains to be seen what effect the Big Four’s growing presence in law will have on larger issues of lawyer professionalism, client service, and public policy.

For now, we simply conclude by urging both practitioners and commentators to pay greater attention to what these important players are doing—and, equally as important, to what law firms, clients, and regulators are, or should be, doing in response.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The article makes no substantive AI-specific claims. Wilkins and Esteban Ferrer argue that the Big Four have rebuilt their legal networks and could reshape corporate legal services around globally integrated, multidisciplinary business solutions.
pts.d: The January/February 2016 article concerns the Big Four's legal-services expansion, rather than AI. The authors claim that these networks have expanded geographically and beyond tax into compliance, finance, M&A and employment law; increasingly integrated legal work with other professional services; and become more visible internationally. They predict that demand for integrated business advice, regulatory liberalisation, organisational capabilities and emerging-market growth will support further expansion. They argue that law firms' adoption of similar business methods may reinforce the Big Four's competitive position. Their narrower technology claim is that process-management and IT capabilities helped the Big Four enter work abandoned by traditional firms, and that alliances with technology companies will prepare them for technological disruption. They do not specify AI applications, automation effects or AI-related employment changes. The AI-related titles appended to the page are separate content listings, not claims made in this article.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is longitudinal website research and press material documenting promoted services and organisational ambitions, not independently verified delivery or performance.
pts.d: The authors examined the Big Four's main websites and 491 location sites between July 2011 and March 2012, searched for affiliated or strategic-partner law firms and relevant press coverage, and repeated the search in November 2015. They report that in spring 2012 PwC promoted legal services in 124 countries, Deloitte in 97, KPMG in 73 and EY in 29. They also report a 200 percent increase between March 2012 and November 2015 in countries where EY promoted a broad range of legal practices. Additional support includes reported lateral recruitment, integration and rebranding of affiliated firms, ABS applications and licences, external rankings, investment announcements, and published legal-market estimates. The authors' explanation of competitive advantages and future growth is an interpretation of these developments, not a causal test. The technology discussion relies on announced PwC–Google for Work and EY–LinkedIn alliances, not measured effects on legal work.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Observed expansion concerns the post-SOX period through 2015; future growth and market transformation are conditional predictions extending into the following years and decades.
pts.d: Writing in 2016, the authors distinguish the rebuilding of legal networks over the preceding decade from expectations of further penetration in the decades ahead. Their forecast depends on continued demand for integrated global advice, regulatory openings, emerging-market opportunities and the Big Four's ability to deliver their promised services. They explicitly acknowledge that local regulation remains important, that promotional claims do not establish actual delivery, and that the ultimate effects on professionalism, client service and public policy remain unresolved. A scenario based on capturing 1 percent of the forecast $726.2 billion global legal market in 2019 illustrates potential scale; it is not a prediction that any network will obtain that share. The technology alliances have no specified impact date, and their legal-business effects are expressly uncertain.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are multinational corporate clients, traditional business law firms, the Big Four's legal-service professionals and legal regulators.
pts.d: For corporate clients, the authors describe an offering that combines legal advice with tax, finance, consulting and industry expertise across jurisdictions, responding to pressure for value for money. For traditional law firms, they foresee stronger competition both in recurring legal matters and higher-value work at the intersection of law and business, alongside competition for experienced lawyers. Within the Big Four, lawyers work across legal service lines, industry groups, geographic units and client teams rather than solely in standalone legal practices. Emerging economies in Asia-Pacific, Latin America and Africa are identified as especially important growth markets. Corporate clients not audited by the relevant Big Four firm are described as an engine of legal-practice growth because audit-client restrictions do not apply to them in the same way. Regulators and the public face unresolved questions about independence, professional values and public policy. The article does not claim AI-driven job displacement or improved access to justice.
